prompt: Ubuntu, Rocky and Alpine all run the same kernel. What makes them different distributions?
hint: Four things are bundled around the kernel. Two of them barely vary.

choices.text: Each patches the kernel so heavily that they diverge
choices.why: They each carry patches, and the kernel is still recognisably the same one.

choices.text: They target different processor architectures
choices.why: All three run on the same hardware. Architecture is a separate axis.

choices.text: The userland, the package manager, and the defaults around them
choices.why: And the fourth is the biggest: how new the software is, how long it is supported, what is on by default.

choices.text: They implement different versions of POSIX
choices.why: POSIX is the floor all of them meet. It is not where they disagree.

prompt: Somebody suggests a distribution you have never heard of. What is the useful question?
hint: Not whether it is good.

choices.text: Which desktop environment does it ship with
choices.why: A preference, and reversible in an afternoon.

choices.text: Who will be publishing its security updates in four years
choices.why: Bundling is cheap; maintaining is not, and that is what the ones that lasted did.

choices.text: How many packages are in its repositories
choices.why: A large number tells you little about whether the ones you need are current.

choices.text: Whether it is based on Debian or Red Hat
choices.why: Worth knowing, and it answers what you type rather than whether to trust it.

prompt: Fill the blank: the commands — `ls`, `grep`, `bash` — are collectively the ___, and on most distributions they come from GNU.
hint: One word, and Alpine replaces it with busybox.

prompt: Which of these are decided by a distribution's policy rather than by its code? Choose all that apply.
hint: Policy is the category that sounds soft and decides what a machine is like to live with.

choices.text: How old the software in a stable release is
choices.why: Debian ships years-old versions on purpose; Arch ships this week's.

choices.text: How long the release is supported
choices.why: Five years, ten, or until the next one six months from now.

choices.text: Whether a firewall is enabled by default
choices.why: A default, and it differs between families.

choices.text: Whether a program compiled elsewhere can run on it
choices.why: That is the kernel interface and the C library, which is code rather than policy.

choices.text: Which system calls the kernel offers
choices.why: The same kernel offers the same calls everywhere.

prompt: A machine reports `ID_LIKE=debian`. What do you already know about it?
hint: The family decides four things before you look at anything else.

choices.text: Its desktop environment and its default browser
choices.why: Neither follows from the family, and both are easy to change.

choices.text: How long it will be supported
choices.why: That is the distribution's own policy, and derivatives vary widely.

choices.text: Which kernel version it runs
choices.why: The family says nothing about the kernel version.

choices.text: `apt`, `.deb`, `apache2` and AppArmor
choices.why: Package manager, package format, service names and security framework — which is most of what you needed.

prompt: Why can you not install a `.deb` package on Rocky Linux?
hint: The family decides the format, and Rocky is in the other one.

choices.text: Rocky is in the Red Hat family, which uses `.rpm`
choices.why: Conversion tools exist and are a last resort, which lesson 7 says out loud.

choices.text: `.deb` packages are compiled for a different architecture
choices.why: Architecture is separate, and the same `.deb` fails on Rocky on the same hardware.

choices.text: Rocky refuses packages it did not build itself
choices.why: It installs plenty of third-party `.rpm` packages happily.

choices.text: The kernel rejects binaries packaged by Debian
choices.why: The kernel never sees the package. The package manager does.

prompt: Match each family to its package manager.
hint: Four families, four tools, and two of them share a package format.
right_distractors: `snap`, which is a second system beside one of these

prompt: Which of these descends from nobody — it was written from scratch rather than derived?
hint: Three of the four have a parent in the tree.

choices.text: Ubuntu
choices.why: Built on Debian, which is the largest derivation in the tree.

choices.text: Rocky Linux
choices.why: Rebuilt from RHEL's sources, source for source.

choices.text: Alpine
choices.why: An independent, and the one you meet inside containers without choosing it.

choices.text: Manjaro
choices.why: Built on Arch, and inherits `pacman` from it.

prompt: Which of these Ubuntu versions is an LTS?
hint: Every LTS is an April release of an even year.

choices.why: October, and an odd year. Nine months of support.
April of an even year, so five years of support and ten with a subscription.
October again, and the same nine-month window.
April, and an odd year, which is what disqualifies it.

prompt: On an Ubuntu 24.04 machine, `cat /etc/debian_version` answers `trixie/sid`. What is going on?
hint: Ask which question that file was built to answer.

choices.text: The machine was upgraded from Debian and kept the old file
choices.why: Nothing was upgraded. A fresh Ubuntu install has that file with that kind of content.

choices.text: Somebody edited it, and it should be corrected
choices.why: It is written by the packaging, and correcting it would be fighting the wrong thing.

choices.text: Ubuntu is Debian, so both answers describe one system
choices.why: They are separate distributions with separate releases, which is why the answers differ.

choices.text: It records the Debian snapshot this Ubuntu was built from
choices.why: Read as "which system am I on" it is wrong, which is why `/etc/os-release` exists.

prompt: You inherit a machine and find four files in `/etc/apt/sources.list.d/`. Why is that worth reading?
hint: Lesson 1 said the risk moved outside the repository. This directory is where it moved to.

choices.text: Each is a third party this machine will trust and install from
choices.why: Ubuntu's own, Docker's and two PPAs is four separate decisions somebody made.

choices.text: It tells you how much disk the package cache is using
choices.why: Cache size lives elsewhere, and these files are configuration rather than data.

choices.text: It lists the packages currently installed
choices.why: Installed packages are a different query, and `dpkg` answers it.

choices.text: It shows which releases the machine can be upgraded to
choices.why: Upgrade paths are not what these files describe.

prompt: Fill the blank: the file that answers "which distribution and which family" on every distribution is ___.
hint: One path, and it replaced the per-family files that came before it.

prompt: What changed about CentOS in late 2020?
hint: It moved to the other side of RHEL.

choices.text: It was discontinued, with no replacement
choices.why: Rocky and Alma were founded within months, both doing what it had done.

choices.text: It became a paid product with a support contract
choices.why: It stayed free. What changed was its position in the pipeline.

choices.text: It became CentOS Stream, upstream of RHEL
choices.why: A preview of the next RHEL minor release, rather than a rebuild of the current one.

choices.text: It merged with Fedora
choices.why: Fedora is upstream and separate, and still is.

prompt: You are reading a 2019 tutorial written for CentOS 7, and your server is Rocky 9. How much applies?
hint: Ask what a rebuild reproduces.

choices.text: Very little — they are different families with different tools
choices.why: They are the same family. Rocky exists precisely to be RHEL-compatible.

choices.text: Most of it — the commands did not change
choices.why: Rocky is binary-compatible with RHEL, which is what it was founded to be.

choices.text: The whole tutorial, word for word
choices.why: Repository URLs and some package names moved, and the version gap is four major releases.

choices.text: Hardly any, because CentOS 7 is out of support
choices.why: Being out of support is about updates, not about whether instructions read correctly.

prompt: On Rocky, `ls -l` shows a file readable by everyone, and the web server still cannot read it. What should you suspect first?
hint: This family enables a second permission system by default.

choices.text: The filesystem is mounted without write access
choices.why: That refuses writes, and this is a read that failed.

choices.text: The web server is running as a user with no groups
choices.why: Its groups are visible, and the file is world-readable anyway.

choices.text: The path contains a directory the web server may not enter
choices.why: Worth checking, and on this family it is the second thing to check rather than the first.

choices.text: SELinux, which can deny what the permission bits allow
choices.why: The denial is logged, and disabling SELinux is the habit every forum teaches and lesson 4 refuses.

prompt: Fill the blank: the Red Hat family's package manager is ___, and `yum` is usually kept as a link to it so old instructions keep working.
hint: Three letters.

prompt: `zypper patch` does something the other families have no single command for. What?
hint: One of the two verbs moves versions and one does not.

choices.text: It rebuilds the package index from the mirrors
choices.why: That is `zypper refresh`, and it touches no installed software.

choices.text: It rolls the machine back to the last snapshot
choices.why: Snapshots are Btrfs and the boot menu, and they are a separate feature.

choices.text: It applies the issued fixes, leaving versions alone
choices.why: `update` moves packages forward; `patch` applies fixes — a genuinely different operation in production.

choices.text: It installs each package the vendor recommends
choices.why: Recommendations are a resolution setting, not what this verb is for.

prompt: SUSE and Red Hat both use `.rpm`. Which of these does SUSE do differently?
hint: One row of section 30's table does not follow the package format.

choices.text: It uses AppArmor rather than SELinux
choices.why: The security framework does not follow the package format, which is the cross-family fact worth carrying.

choices.text: Its packages are incompatible with `rpm`
choices.why: Both use `.rpm`, and `rpm` reads them.

choices.text: It has no long-term supported release
choices.why: SLE is a long-support enterprise product, and Leap is built from the same sources.

choices.text: Its web server package is called `httpd`
choices.why: It is `apache2` on SUSE, which is the Debian side's name rather than Red Hat's.

prompt: A scanner says your `nginx 1.18` is vulnerable. The distribution says it is patched. Who is right?
hint: Ask what a fixed release does with a fix, and what it does with the version number.

choices.text: The scanner — the distribution has not shipped the fix yet
choices.why: The fix was applied weeks ago. What did not move is the number.

choices.text: The distribution — the fix was backported
choices.why: Which is why comparing version numbers is not a reliable way to judge a fixed release.

choices.text: Both, for different vulnerabilities
choices.why: Nothing in the situation suggests two separate issues.

choices.text: Neither — the version is too old to be supported
choices.why: 1.18 in a supported release is supported. Age is the model, not a defect.

prompt: Match each distribution to its release model.
hint: Three models, and one of them means there is no version number to ask about.

pairs.right: Fixed — frozen at release, security fixes only
Fixed, with a five to ten year window
Rolling — always current, and no version
Fixed, with a window of about thirteen months

right_distractors: Built from source by each user at install time
Released only when a paying customer requests one

prompt: A server reaches end of life. What happens on that day?
hint: Ask what stops, rather than what breaks.

choices.text: Services refuse to start until the system is upgraded
choices.why: Nothing refuses. That is what makes this dangerous.

choices.text: The package manager blocks further installs
choices.why: It keeps working, against repositories that have stopped moving.

choices.text: The machine shuts down and has to be reinstalled
choices.why: No distribution does this, and it would be a strange thing to build.

choices.text: Nothing visible — and the security updates stop
choices.why: The machine works perfectly while accumulating published, unpatched vulnerabilities.

prompt: On an end-of-life release, `apt upgrade` reports that everything is up to date. What does that mean?
hint: The sentence is true and the reassurance is not.

choices.text: The machine is fully patched and needs no attention
choices.why: It is patched up to the last update ever published for it, which is not the same thing.

choices.text: The package index is stale and needs refreshing
choices.why: Refreshing an index that has stopped moving returns the same answer.

choices.text: No more updates are ever coming
choices.why: The failure mode of a lifecycle is silence, which is the same shape as a scheduled job that stopped running.

choices.text: The repositories have been removed from the machine
choices.why: They are still configured; they simply have nothing new in them.

prompt: Fill the blank: an Ubuntu release like `24.10`, which is not an LTS, is supported for only ___ months.
hint: A single number, and it is shorter than many deployment plans.

prompt: A script that works on your Ubuntu machine fails inside an Alpine container, on a flag that looks like it should exist. What is it?
hint: Alpine replaces the userland, not just the package manager.

choices.text: The container is missing the package that provides the command
choices.why: The command ran — it rejected a flag, which means it was found and started.

choices.text: Alpine uses busybox, whose commands implement the common uses and not the GNU extensions
choices.why: A smaller `ls`, not a broken container.

choices.text: The script needs to be marked executable inside the container
choices.why: That refuses differently, and before any flag is read.

choices.text: Alpine mounts the filesystem without write access, so the flag was refused
choices.why: It does not, and a read-only mount refuses writes rather than flags.

prompt: A Python package installs into an Alpine image and then fails to load, with an error about a shared object. What is the likely cause?
hint: Something below the package manager was replaced.

choices.text: The package was built for a different Python version
choices.why: Possible in general, and it would name the version rather than a shared object.

choices.text: The image ran out of disk while installing
choices.why: That fails during install, loudly, rather than at load time.

choices.text: `apk` installed it without its dependencies
choices.why: `apk` resolves dependencies, as every package manager in this lesson does.

choices.text: It is a prebuilt binary linked against glibc, and Alpine uses musl
choices.why: Nothing in the message says musl, which is why the shape is worth recognising.

prompt: A Dockerfile line reads `apk add --no-cache curl`. What is the flag for?
hint: The whole design of this distribution is one property.

choices.text: It leaves no package index on disk, keeping the image small
choices.why: Size is bandwidth and money, multiplied by every machine that pulls the image.

choices.text: It skips the signature check to make the build faster
choices.why: Skipping verification is not what it does, and would be a poor trade.

choices.text: It refuses to use a locally cached copy of the package
choices.why: The cache it means is the index left behind, not a copy of the package.

choices.text: It installs the package without its dependencies
choices.why: Dependencies are resolved either way.

prompt: Which of these are true of Alpine? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two replacements, and each has a consequence you will meet.

choices.text: `/bin/sh` is busybox's ash, and there is no bash unless you install it
choices.why: A script beginning `#!/bin/bash` fails outright.

choices.text: It uses musl rather than glibc
choices.why: Which is why a binary compiled elsewhere refuses to start.

choices.text: Its package manager is `apk`
choices.why: The fifth in this lesson, and the one in every Dockerfile example.

choices.text: It is derived from Debian
choices.why: It descends from nobody. It is one of the independents.

choices.text: It runs systemd like the other families
choices.why: It uses OpenRC, and section 30 notes this as part of why it gets its own section.

prompt: `systemctl restart apache2` on Rocky answers that there is no such service, and the web server is running. Why?
hint: The software is identical. The name is not.

choices.text: Apache was downloaded but not installed
choices.why: A running web server was installed by something.

choices.text: The service needs `sudo` before it can be named
choices.why: Without `sudo` it refuses on permission, and names the permission.

choices.text: On Red Hat it is `httpd`, with its config in `/etc/httpd`
choices.why: The clearest example of what a family buys you: same software, different name to type.

choices.text: Rocky replaces Apache with nginx by default
choices.why: It installs whichever you asked for, and nginx is `nginx` everywhere.

prompt: Which of these are the same across Debian, Red Hat and SUSE? Choose all that apply.
hint: The list of differences is short, and that is the useful fact.

choices.text: `grep`, `sed`, `awk`, pipes and redirection
choices.why: Lesson 8 applies unchanged on all of them.

choices.text: `systemctl` and `journalctl`
choices.why: Lesson 5 applies to every family here — Alpine is the exception, and it uses OpenRC.

choices.text: The permission bits, users and groups
choices.why: Lesson 4 applies everywhere, and SELinux sits above them rather than replacing them.

choices.text: The package manager
choices.why: `apt`, `dnf` and `zypper` — the first row of the table.

choices.text: The firewall front end
choices.why: `ufw` against `firewalld`, and both are wrappers over the same machinery.

prompt: You were given `apt install nginx` and your machine is SUSE. What do you type?
hint: Notice how much of the line survives.

choices.text: `apt-get install nginx`
choices.why: A different spelling of the same tool, which SUSE does not have either.

choices.text: `zypper install nginx`
choices.why: The verb and the package name survive; the first word is what changed.

choices.text: `dnf install nginx`
choices.why: That is the Red Hat family's tool, and SUSE is its own.

choices.text: `apk add nginx`
choices.why: That is Alpine's, and it changes the verb as well as the tool.

prompt: Fill the blank: on the Red Hat family a second permission system called ___ is enabled by default, and it can deny what the permission bits allow.
hint: Seven letters, and every forum answer tells you to switch it off.

prompt: Which field of `/etc/os-release` tells you what to type — the package manager, the service names, the security framework?
hint: One field names the distribution and one names the family.

choices.text: `ID`
choices.why: It names the distribution, which is useful and narrower than what you asked.

choices.text: `ID_LIKE`
choices.why: A distribution you have never heard of that says `debian` is one whose commands you already know.

choices.text: `VERSION_ID`
choices.why: It answers whether the machine is still supported, which is section 30's question.

choices.text: `PRETTY_NAME`
choices.why: It is the human label, and it is for reading rather than for deciding.

prompt: Debian's own `/etc/os-release` has no `ID_LIKE` field at all. What does the absence tell you?
hint: The field says what a distribution resembles.

choices.text: The file is incomplete and the distribution should fix it
choices.why: It is complete. The field is optional and its absence is meaningful.

choices.text: Debian predates the standard and skipped it
choices.why: It adopted it, and the file is there with the other fields filled in.

choices.text: The machine was installed from a minimal image
choices.why: Image size does not change which fields this file carries.

choices.text: Debian is a family head — it is not like anything else
choices.why: Absence is information: nothing upstream to fall back on.

prompt: Inside a container, `hostnamectl` answers that the system was not booted with systemd. Why is `/etc/os-release` the better habit?
hint: One of the two is a file.

choices.text: It is read straight off disk, with no service in the way
choices.why: `hostnamectl` is part of systemd, and a container booted nothing.

choices.text: `hostnamectl` needs root and `cat` does not
choices.why: Neither needs root here, and the refusal names the bus rather than a permission.

choices.text: `hostnamectl` reports the kernel rather than the distribution
choices.why: It reports both, when it can answer at all.

choices.text: The file is updated more often than `hostnamectl`'s source
choices.why: They read the same facts. One of them can be read without a service.

prompt: `uname -a` prints `Linux vm 6.18.44-fc-v24 ... x86_64`. Which question did it answer?
hint: It is not the distribution.

choices.text: Which distribution and which version this machine runs
choices.why: Nothing in that line names a distribution. `/etc/os-release` is where that lives.

choices.text: Which packages are installed
choices.why: A different query entirely, and the package manager answers it.

choices.text: Which kernel and which processor architecture
choices.why: And the hostname. It is what to ask when software requires a particular kernel or architecture.

choices.text: How long the machine has been running
choices.why: That is `uptime`, and it is a different command.

prompt: You reach a machine you did not set up. What is the first command?
hint: It changes nothing, and it answers six questions at once.

choices.text: `uptime`, to see how long it has been running
choices.why: Interesting and it tells you nothing about what to type next.

choices.text: `sudo apt update`, to make sure the index is current
choices.why: It assumes the family before you have checked it, which is the mistake this lesson exists to prevent.

choices.text: `uname -a`, to see the kernel
choices.why: A different question, and one you ask second.

choices.text: `cat /etc/os-release`
choices.why: Distribution, family and version, in two seconds, changing nothing.

prompt: Match each symptom to the distribution family it points at.
hint: Four situations, and each one names its family by what it does rather than by a label.

pairs.left: `systemctl restart apache2` says there is no such service
`ls --human-readable` is rejected as an unknown option
The file is world-readable and the web server still cannot read it
pairs.right: Red Hat — SELinux above the bits

pairs.left: `zypper patch` applies fixes without moving versions
pairs.right: SUSE — the verb no other family has

right_distractors: Debian — the volunteer project with a constitution
Arch — rolling, and assembled by hand

prompt: Your production servers run CentOS 7. What is the situation?
hint: The date passed in June 2024.

choices.text: Supported for another two years under the extended window
choices.why: The extended window ended with the standard one.

choices.text: Out of support since 2024, and still serving
choices.why: The failure mode is silence, and `yum update` reports everything up to date.

choices.text: Automatically migrated to CentOS Stream by the last update
choices.why: Nothing migrates a machine by itself, and Stream is a different position in the pipeline.

choices.text: Fine, because CentOS was a rebuild rather than a product
choices.why: Being a rebuild did not extend its dates; it inherited RHEL 7's.

prompt: Fill the blank: the field in `/etc/os-release` that names the family, and therefore what you type, is ___.
hint: Two words joined by an underscore.

prompt: You are building a container image for a Go binary. Which base image, and why?
hint: Ask what the program needs from the distribution.

choices.text: Ubuntu LTS, for the long support window
choices.why: A support window is about a machine you maintain, and this image is rebuilt every deploy.

choices.text: Rocky, so it matches the production servers
choices.why: Base image and host distribution are independent for a static binary.

choices.text: Alpine — the binary does not care, and size is bandwidth
choices.why: A Go binary drags no prebuilt native code behind it, which is exactly when Alpine is the right answer.

choices.text: Debian slim, because Alpine runs no compiled programs
choices.why: It runs them; what it refuses are binaries linked against glibc.

prompt: A colleague asks which distribution is best. What is the useful reply?
hint: The lesson's closing argument.

choices.text: Support window, size, and ecosystem
choices.why: None of those is "best". Section 33 works three cases and reaches three answers.

choices.text: Ubuntu, because it has the largest community
choices.why: Community size is real and does not settle a production decision.

choices.text: Whichever has the newest packages
choices.why: That is one model of three, and it is the wrong one for a server.

choices.text: Whichever the person asking already knows
choices.why: Familiarity counts and does not answer a ten-year deployment.

prompt: `cat /etc/debian_version` on a machine answers `trixie/sid`. Can you conclude it is Debian?
hint: Section 25 showed this exact file on a machine that is not Debian.

choices.text: Yes — that file is Debian's and nobody else's
choices.why: Ubuntu ships it too, which is the entire trap.

choices.text: Yes, and the codename tells you which release
choices.why: The codename is a Debian one and the machine may be something built from it.

choices.text: Yes, provided the machine also has `apt` installed
choices.why: Ubuntu has `apt` as well, so that narrows nothing.

choices.text: No — Ubuntu carries that file too
choices.why: Which is why `/etc/os-release` exists: one file, same fields, every distribution.

prompt: You must run a company web server for the next eight years. Which factors decide? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three of the five are the ones section 33 actually uses.

choices.text: The length of the support window
choices.why: Eight years rules out anything with a nine-month or thirteen-month window.

choices.text: Whether the software you run publishes packages for that family
choices.why: Vendors frequently publish for Red Hat and nothing else.

choices.text: Who your team can already operate
choices.why: Familiarity is a real operational cost, not a preference.

choices.text: Which distribution has the newest kernel
choices.why: A server wants boring, and a fixed release backports what matters.

choices.text: Which has the nicest desktop environment
choices.why: A server has no desktop, which lesson 1 section 04 already said.

prompt: You inherit a server. Put the first four checks in the order the lesson recommends.
items: Check its version against the support dates — is it still receiving updates
Translate the command you were about to run into that family's spelling
trap: The common mistake is putting the translation first, from a family you assumed. Assuming is the failure this lesson is built to prevent — the command you were given was written for somebody else's machine.

prompt: Fill the blank: Alpine replaces glibc with ___, which is why a binary compiled elsewhere refuses to start in it.
hint: Four letters.
